sections.title: Front matter

summary.text: The front matter of the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, with cataloguing data, joint copyright and ISBNs for both organizations. It includes the foreword, acknowledgements and an overview of the toolkit's three parts on developing a national eHealth vision, an action plan and a monitoring framework. It ends with tables of contents and lists of figures and tables.

sections.title: National context for eHealth

summary.text: Opens the chapter on national context by making the case for eHealth as central to responsive health systems and giving WHO's definition of eHealth as the use of ICT for health. It describes how eHealth supports care delivery, workforce, programme management and research. It notes international commitments to eHealth and the need for national strategies to coordinate efforts.

sections.extract: 1.1 The case for eHealth1 eHealth is changing health-care delivery today and is at the core of responsive health systems. The daily business of health relies on information and communication and, increasingly, on the technologies that enable it, at every level and in every country. This is equally so in delivering care, deploying personnel, managing programmes or conducting research. The World Health Organization

summary.text: Describes how a country's eHealth context can be classed by the maturity of its ICT and enabling environments, from experimentation and early adoption through building up to scaling up and mainstreaming. It explains what each stage involves and how strategy priorities differ. Actions include using information for public health planning, protecting privacy and monitoring that eHealth meets health priorities.

sections.title: Framework for a national eHealth vision

summary.text: Opens Chapter 2, explaining that a national eHealth vision sets out why a national approach is needed, what it will achieve and how.

sections.extract: Chapter 2 Framework for a national eHealth vision A national eHealth vision explains why a national approach to eHealth is needed, what a national eHealth plan will achieve, and how it will be done (Figure 3). Answering these questions constitutes the major work of strategy development.

sections.title: National eHealth vision: overview of the method

summary.text: Outlines the toolkit's method for developing a national eHealth vision, based on country experience, starting from an unconstrained draft refined into recommendations that feed the implementation plan.

sections.extract: method The Toolkit method is based on experience and lessons from countries that have already developed a national strategy (Figure 4). A successful outcome requires effective leadership, a well-managed process and stakeholder engagement. sections.title: Sample structure for an initial vision statement

summary.text: Gives a fill-in-the-blanks template for a vision statement linking a timeframe, health system benefits and changes to information flows.

sections.extract: By [timeframe] eHealth will deliver [strategic benefits and outcomes for the health system and population] through [strategic changes to health information flows]. This structure ensures that the vision statement for eHealth can exist in isolation and still communicate the value of investing in a national eHealth environment (Box 4).

summary.text: Presents a sample scenario about Akeyo, a woman in rural east Africa recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, whose family faces a long walk to a health centre with a visiting doctor. It contrasts her experience of the current health system with how eHealth could improve her care. The section advises adding realism by drawing on service examples from Annex A and reviewing scenarios with stakeholders.

sections.title: Gather information on the eHealth environment

summary.text: Covers the stage of gathering information on the existing and planned eHealth environment across the seven component areas, to find chances for reuse and gaps to address. It offers detailed sample questions for each area, from governance bodies and funding to infrastructure, standards, legislation and workforce skills. It describes internal research using existing documents and reports, followed by consultation with a wide range of stakeholders. It stresses that this step is about collecting information, while judging its implications for the vision is left to the next stage.

sections.title: Examples of eHealth

summary.text: Defines common types of eHealth drawn from the WHO Global Observatory for eHealth, including electronic medical records, electronic health records and personal health records. It describes telemedicine forms such as store-and-forward, remote monitoring and interactive services, plus telecare and mobile health. Further entries cover areas such as distance learning for health professionals and health information systems that bring together data on disease, risks and service coverage.

sections.extract: These examples are taken from the Global Observatory for eHealth (http://www.who.int/goe/en). sections.title: Governance continuum

summary.text: Annex F describes a governance continuum for national eHealth, from a centralised, fully regulated bureaucratic model to a decentralised free-market model, with a guided-market model in between. The guided market combines central coordination in areas of national importance with flexibility, competition and incentives elsewhere, and is adapted from an Australian strategy.
